title: robots.txt exists and parses
question: Can an agent fetch /robots.txt and parse it?
method: GET /robots.txt. Pass on a 200 response whose body is a robots file, not HTML (the RFC 9309 parser is lenient, so an empty file passes). Warn on 404 or any other 4xx: crawlers then treat everything as allowed, but intent is unstated. Warn on a 200 that carries an HTML document (often a soft 404): Google then finds no rules and crawls everything, but intent is unstated. Warn when the file is larger than 500 KiB, the part Google reads. Fail on a 500 or another persistent server error, which crawlers treat as disallow all. Skipped as inconclusive on 429, 502, 503, 504 or no response. A warning still meets the Level 1 gate, because crawlers can read the site either way.

spec.title: Google: How Google interprets the robots.txt specification

title: Sitemap declared and reachable
question: Is there a sitemap an agent can fetch?
method: Try the Sitemap: lines from robots.txt, then the usual paths in the order the platform uses them (/wp-sitemap.xml and /sitemap_index.xml first on WordPress, /sitemap.xml first elsewhere; /wp-sitemap.xml only on WordPress), on the store's own origin only and with at most four sitemap requests in all. Discovery stops at the first rate limit or server error, and a home page that refused the scanner gets only the sitemaps robots.txt declares. The first that answers 200 with parseable sitemap XML is used. Pass when it lists at least one URL or child sitemap, warn when it lists neither or when a sitemap file read breaks the protocol limits (a Content-Length above 50 MB, which counts against the uncompressed size, or more than 50,000 entries counted in one file), fail when no candidate answers with a sitemap, naming the paths tried. Skipped as inconclusive when discovery stopped early, because absence is then not established: on a rate limit or server error, on a candidate that gave no response, when the four requests ran out with candidates untried, or when the home page refused the scanner and no sitemap robots.txt declares could be read.

spec.title: Google Search Central: manage large sitemaps with a sitemap index

title: Product URLs in sitemap
question: Does the sitemap list product pages?
method: Read the sitemap found by A1.2 and, in a sitemap index, its child sitemaps with product sitemaps first (WooCommerce wp-sitemap-posts-product-*.xml, product-sitemap.xml, Shopify sitemap_products_1.xml and similar names). Pass when at least one product URL is read: any entry of a product sitemap, or an entry whose path has a product segment such as /product/ or /products/. On a site already checked as a store, where neither matches, entries that share one product-identifier shape (/<slug>/PLID123: a slug, then an identifier with the same letter prefix, for at least 80% of 20 or more entries read) count as product URLs, and the message says so. Warn when the index lists a child sitemap with "product" in its URL but no product URL could be read within the request limit. Fail otherwise. Skipped as inconclusive when sitemap discovery stopped on a rate limit or server error.

title: Link response headers
question: Does the site point agents at its machine-readable resources through Link headers?
method: Read the Link response headers of the home page and one sampled product page, parsed per RFC 8288 (a multi-member header with parameters such as version), and the <link> elements in the home page's head. Pass when a relation an agent can use is present: ucp (the relation Shopify Online Store sends on every response, and which Hydrogen storefronts declare as <link rel="ucp" href="/.well-known/ucp"> in the head, the only relation read from the head), llms-txt, api-catalog, service-desc, describedby, license with type application/rsl+xml, or alternate with type text/markdown. Fail when Link values are present but none carries a relation an agent can use. Skipped as not applicable when there is none at all, because the convention is optional. The only relation a shipping consumer reads today is ucp. The rest are conventions, hence weight 1.

spec.title: Shopify Hydrogen: the rel="ucp" Link header and HTML link (pull request 4153)

title: llms.txt is valid when present
question: If the site publishes llms.txt, is it a usable file?
method: GET /llms.txt. A 404 or 410 skips the check as not applicable: the file is optional and no major assistant documents reading it (Google states that Search does not use it), so its absence is never scored. Skipped as inconclusive on 429, 502, 503, 504 or no response. Any other status than 200 fails. On a 200 the body must be text, not HTML (a soft 404 fails), and must contain an H1 line (# Title), the only element the proposal requires. Warn when it has no Markdown links, pass otherwise. Stricter than Lighthouse on the content type, more lenient on links (Lighthouse fails a file without a Markdown link or under 50 characters).

spec.title: Google: AI features and your website (llms.txt is not used by Search)

title: llms.txt links to the catalog
question: Does llms.txt lead an agent to the catalog as data?
method: When llms.txt is present and valid, pass when one of its Markdown links points at a product feed, a product API, a product sitemap, the shop index, a UCP profile or an MCP endpoint (Shopify's generated file names /.well-known/ucp and /api/ucp/mcp), so an agent that reads the file reaches the catalog as data. Fail when it links only to prose pages, or has no links. Skipped when there is no llms.txt or it failed A1.5. Informational: a convention with no documented reader.

title: Sitemap lastmod is present and plausible
question: Can an agent tell from the sitemap what changed and when?
method: Read <lastmod> in the first 5,000 entries of the sitemaps fetched. Pass when at least 80 percent of entries carry a valid W3C datetime and the values differ from one another. Warn when fewer entries carry one, or when every value is identical (a timestamp generated at request time, which crawlers learn to ignore). Fail when none carry a valid one. Skipped when no sitemap was found or the sitemaps list no URL entries. Bing names lastmod a key signal for how fast changes reach its AI answers, and Google uses it when it is consistently accurate.

spec.title: Bing: keeping content discoverable with sitemaps in AI-powered search

title: Listing pages link to products and further pages
question: Can a crawler walk from a category page to every product and to the next page with plain links?
method: GET the sampled listing page (a collection or category page linked from the home page, the most-linked concrete one, never a product page). Count same-origin anchors to product URLs and look for crawlable pagination: a rel=next link, or anchors whose URL names a page number (/page/2/, ?page=2, ?p=2, ?paged=2, ?pg=2). Pass when the page links to two or more products and either paginates with links or has no load-more control. Warn when products are listed but the only way to more of them is a load-more button or infinite scroll (Google's crawlers do not click or scroll, and Bing asks for standard anchor links), when the page links to exactly one product, when no product link is found in the HTML, or when the page cannot be fetched or answers an error. Not applicable when no listing page was found, or when the sampled page is a category index: no product link and three or more links to further category pages.
